Actions to address tuberculosis (TB) diagnosis and treatment may include re-evaluating the patient for TB, conducting additional testing using molecular WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic tests (mWRDs), culturing additional samples, and assessing the possibility of laboratory or clerical errors. If anti-TB therapy was initiated based on clinical judgment, the response to therapy should be carefully evaluated. 2. For mWRD results indicating Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (MTBC) detected, rifampicin (RIF) resistance detected, but phenotypic drug susceptibility testing (DST) shows RIF susceptibility: Use the mWRD result to guide treatment decisions while awaiting further testing. Consider the possibility of a false-susceptible phenotypic result, as strains with certain mutations often fail treatment with RIF-based first-line regimens. 3. In settings with low multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) prevalence, silent mutations may cause false-resistant mWRD results, though these are rare. False RIF-resistant results have been observed with the Xpert MTB/RIF G4 cartridge when the MTBC detected result was very low and associated with probe binding delay. Follow-up actions may include mWRD testing of the culture, DNA sequencing, confirmatory testing on other mWRD platforms, phenotypic DST using solid media, and evaluation of laboratory or clerical errors. 4. For mWRD results indicating MTBC detected, RIF resistance not detected, but phenotypic DST shows RIF resistance: Modify the treatment regimen based on phenotypic DST results. False RIF-susceptible mWRD results are rare but have been observed in 1–5% of RIF-resistant TB cases tested with Xpert MTB/RIF in various epidemiologic settings. Mutations outside the rifampicin resistance-determining region (RRDR) of the rpoB gene may account for these discrepancies. Surveillance to monitor the emergence of such clones over time should be considered. 5. For Xpert Ultra results indicating MTBC detected trace with a negative culture: Interpretation must consider patient characteristics, specimen type, and prior TB treatment history. Negative cultures may result from factors such as prior TB treatment, transport or processing issues, contamination, inadequate testing volume, or laboratory/clerical errors. Small numbers of bacilli in the sample may indicate active TB, laboratory cross-contamination, recent exposure to TB bacilli, or current/past TB treatment. The presence of non-viable or non-replicating bacilli may explain MTBC detected trace results in individuals who completed therapy within the past 4–5 years. Follow-up actions may include assessing the response to therapy, re-evaluating prior or current anti-TB drug use, repeating Xpert Ultra testing, evaluating laboratory/clerical errors, and repeating culture testing (preferably using liquid culture). 6. Algorithm 2 for lateral flow lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) testing is recommended for diagnosing TB in people living with HIV (PLHIV), particularly in high HIV burden settings. LF-LAM results are available within 15 minutes and should guide treatment decisions while awaiting results from other diagnostic tests. LF-LAM has sufficient sensitivity and specificity for diagnosing TB in PLHIV but is less effective in HIV-negative individuals. 7. For hospitalized PLHIV, systematic TB testing with mWRD is recommended in settings where TB prevalence exceeds 10%. LF-LAM testing is emphasized for rapid diagnosis and treatment initiation in critically ill PLHIV. Outpatient settings should also use LF-LAM and mWRD testing in parallel for PLHIV with TB symptoms. 8. Negative LF-LAM or mWRD results do not rule out TB in symptomatic individuals. Additional evaluations, such as chest X-rays, clinical assessments, and further mWRD or culture testing, may be necessary. Treatment for bacterial infections or Pneumocystis pneumonia should be considered, and clinical response should be evaluated after 3–5 days of treatment. 9. For newly diagnosed HIV patients, those returning after treatment interruption, or those with failing antiretroviral therapy (ART) regimens, systematic TB evaluation using LF-LAM and mWRD is recommended.
